text:
**Setting up.** Vertices split into odds $\{1,3,5,7\}$ and evens $\{2,4,6,8\}$. Same‑parity edges have weight $-1$; cross edges $\{i,j\}$ have weight $|j-i|$.

In a perfect matching, the number of odd–odd edges equals the number of even–even edges; call it $k\in\{0,1,2\}$.

Let $B$ be the $4\times 4$ matrix of cross‑edge weights (rows = odds $1,3,5,7$, columns = evens $2,4,6,8$):
$$
B=\begin{pmatrix}1&3&5&7\\1&1&3&5\\3&1&1&3\\5&3&1&1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

**Case $k=0$** (all four edges cross): sum $=\operatorname{perm}(B)$.

Expanding along the first row, the $3\times3$ minors have permanents $54, 98, 98, 54$, so
$$\operatorname{perm}(B)=1\cdot54+3\cdot98+5\cdot98+7\cdot54=54+294+490+378=1216.$$
(Checked by listing all 24 permutations: subtotals $54,294,490,378$.)

**Case $k=1$**: one odd–odd edge and one even–even edge (product $(-1)^2=+1$), plus two cross edges. Summing over the two ways to match the remaining two odds with the remaining two evens gives the permanent of a $2\times2$ submatrix of $B$; summing over all choices gives the sum of permanents of all $2\times2$ submatrices of $B$:
$$\sum_{i<i'}\Big(R_iR_{i'}-\mathbf r_i\cdot \mathbf r_{i'}\Big)$$
with row sums $R=(16,10,8,10)$ and dot products $54,32,26,22,16,22$:
$$(160-54)+(128-32)+(160-26)+(80-22)+(100-16)+(80-22)=106+96+134+58+84+58=536.$$

**Case $k=2$**: two odd–odd and two even–even edges, weight $(-1)^4=1$; there are $3\cdot3=9$ such matchings, contributing $9$.

(Check of counts: $24+72+9=105$.)

**Total:** $1216+536+9=1761$.

ANSWER: 1761
